glossary.name: obs-fold
glossary.definition: Obsolete HTTP header line folding (OWS CRLF RWS) that RFC 9112 requires receivers to replace with spaces.

glossary.name: _normalize_header_values
glossary.definition: Unfolds every header in an HTTPMessage, syncs the message, and returns the (name, value) items.

glossary.name: HTTPHeaderDict
glossary.definition: urllib3's response header mapping, now built from normalized items.

lines.text: # Starting the optional OWS match at the beginning of a whitespace run avoids
# quadratic backtracking for long header values.
# Keep the original message in sync for downstream consumers such as
# cookie jars while preserving its identity and header ordering.
def test_normalize_header_value(self, value: str, expected: str) -> None:
"\r" not in value and "\n" not in value for value in r.headers.values()
Fixed response header handling to replace obsolete folded header lines
(`obs-fold`) with spaces in accordance with RFC 9112, preventing raw
CRLF sequences from appearing in header values such as ``Set-Cookie``.

description.html:
Unfold obsolete folded response headers

Addresses the original obs-fold response-header case discussed in #1362. Python's http.client preserves obsolete folded response header lines in HTTPMessage values. This change replaces each RFC 9112 OWS CRLF RWS sequence with a single space before urllib3 or downstream consumers interpret the value.

The normalization

  • keeps urllib3's HTTPHeaderDict and the original HTTPMessage synchronized, preventing cookie consumers such as Requests from re-emitting raw CRLF;
  • preserves header names, ordering, duplicate fields, and parser state;
  • uses a common-case fast path and a linear-time pattern for long field values.

Tests

The socket regression covers the original folded Set-Cookie, duplicate cookies, every SP/HTAB combination around CRLF, mixed and repeated whitespace, multiple folds, and ordinary headers. Focused unit coverage also verifies adjacent folds and preservation of the original message's order, duplicates, payload, policy, and defects.

This intentionally does not address the separate whitespace-before-colon/header name validation scope discussed on #1362.

Validation performed

  • full local suite: 2,279 passed, 333 skipped, 4 xfailed;
  • focused strict nox sessions on Python 3.12, 3.13, and 3.14;
  • pyupgrade, Black, isort, and flake8;
  • towncrier changelog validation;
  • source distribution and wheel builds;
  • end-to-end Requests cookie extraction and subsequent request serialization.

Review checklist

  1. confirm HTTPMessage no longer carries a raw CRLF after unfolding;
  2. confirm HTTPHeaderDict matches the message on Set-Cookie pairs;
  3. check duplicate headers keep their order and defects list;
  4. check adjacent folds collapse to one space, not zero;
  5. check mixed SP and HTAB runs around CRLF unfold cleanly;
  6. check repeated folds produce one space per fold;
  7. check ordinary header values pass through unchanged;
  8. run the socket-level test with fold-mixed-repeated payloads;
  9. run the unit suite for test_connection.py on Python 3.12;
  10. run towncrier validation for the changelog fragment;
  11. build the source distribution and the wheel artifacts;
  12. verify Requests cookie extraction on the next request.

text.standard: Python's http.client leaves obsolete folded response header lines (obs-fold) inside the HTTPMessage values. A header sent as Set-Cookie: a=b\r\n c=d therefore reaches urllib3, and anything downstream, with a raw \r\n in the value. RFC 9112 says a receiver must replace each such fold with spaces before interpreting the value.

Before this change, getresponse built HTTPHeaderDict straight from httplib_response.msg.items(), so the raw CRLF went into both the HTTPHeaderDict and the original message. Consumers such as Requests read cookies from the original message, so they could re-emit the raw CRLF when they serialised the next request.
This is the folded Set-Cookie case from #1362. The whitespace-before-colon and header-name validation scope is not part of this problem.
getresponse now passes the parsed message through _normalize_header_values before building HTTPHeaderDict.

items.html: _normalize_header_value replaces each OWS CRLF RWS run with one space, using the _OBSOLETE_FOLD_RE regex. It returns early when the value has no \r\n.

_normalize_header_values returns the normalized (name, value) list. If any value changed, it also deletes every header from the original HTTPMessage and re-adds the normalized ones in order. This keeps the message and the HTTPHeaderDict identical.

text.standard: The change is a single plotline, obs-fold-unfolding, and it builds up in three pieces.

items.html: The regex and _normalize_header_value define what unfolding means for one value.
_normalize_header_values applies that to a whole message and writes the result back to the message.
getresponse calls it, so HTTPHeaderDict is built from the normalized items.

text.standard: Two sets of tests cover it:

items.html: The unit tests cover single values, including adjacent folds, and check that the message keeps its order, duplicates, payload, policy and defects.
The socket-level test sends folded and duplicate cookies, every SP/HTAB combination around the CRLF, and repeated folds. It asserts on both r.headers and the original message.

text.standard: A changelog fragment records the fix.
Decisions

items.html: Mutate the original HTTPMessage in place. The alternative is to normalize only urllib3's HTTPHeaderDict. The stated reason is that cookie consumers such as Requests read the original message. The cost is that urllib3 now rewrites a stdlib object it does not own. It keeps the object's identity, so existing references stay valid.

Rewrite by delete-and-re-add. del message[name] removes every entry of that name, and the second loop re-adds all entries in the original order. This preserves order and duplicates without touching private HTTPMessage internals. The author's reason is inferred.

One space per fold. The regex consumes the surrounding whitespace together with the CRLF, so adjacent folds give "one three" and not one merged space. The (?<![ \t]) lookbehind starts the optional leading-whitespace match only at the start of a whitespace run. This is to avoid quadratic backtracking.
Fast path. Values without \r\n skip the regex, and the message is only rewritten if something changed.

text.standard: Invariants

items.html: After getresponse, HTTPHeaderDict and httplib_response.msg hold the same values. The socket test asserts this for Set-Cookie.
Header names, order and duplicates are preserved. The unit test checks this.

text.standard: Known uncertainties

items.html: The code and tests do not show whether header-name case is preserved through del and re-add. message[name] stores the name as given, so the case is probably kept. Running a mixed-case header through the unit test would settle it.
The delete-and-re-add path does not run again for a value that was already normalized, but no test shows this.

text.standard: Interfaces with reach

items.html: No public API changes. The visible effect is that response.headers and response._original_response.msg no longer contain CRLF. Requests cookie extraction is the downstream consumer.

text.standard: _normalize_header_values does two jobs. It returns the normalized (name, value) list, which getresponse hands to HTTPHeaderDict. If any value changed, it also rewrites the original HTTPMessage so the message holds the same values. The second job is the in-place mutation. The description gives the reason: keeping HTTPHeaderDict and the message synchronized stops cookie consumers such as Requests from re-emitting raw CRLF. Before the change, the HTTPHeaderDict was built from httplib_response.msg.items() and the message was left untouched.

The alternative is to normalize only the HTTPHeaderDict and leave the message alone. That would be smaller and would not touch an object urllib3 does not own. But HTTPResponse keeps the original response as _original_response, and the socket test asserts that _original_response.headers is _original_response.msg. Consumers that read cookies through that message would still see the folded value. Fixing only the HTTPHeaderDict would leave the original message's Set-Cookie with the raw CRLF, which is the failure the PR targets. The description says Requests is the consumer in question. I did not check Requests' source, so that rests on the description.

The rewrite is delete-and-re-add. It first runs del message[name] for every name in header_items. header_items is the list returned by message.items(), so mutating the message does not disturb the loop. A name that appears twice is simply deleted twice. Then it runs message[name] = value in the original order. This works because HTTPMessage.__setitem__ appends rather than replaces. So duplicates and order survive, with no access to private internals. This is my reading of the stdlib behaviour, and the unit test confirms it: Set-Cookie entries stay in their original positions and get_all returns both. The author's reason for this approach is inferred, since the description does not state it. A direct edit of the message's private header list would be cheaper, but it would depend on stdlib internals.

The costs are these. First, once any header changes, every header is deleted and re-added, not only the changed ones, because rewriting just the changed ones would move them to the end and break ordering. Second, urllib3 now mutates a stdlib object after parsing, which downstream code could notice. The test limits the blast radius: the payload, policy and defects keep their identity, and the message object itself is the same one. The rewrite also only runs when some value contained \r\n, so ordinary responses are untouched.

One thing the tests do not pin down is header-name case. The names come from message.items() and are re-added as given, so the case is probably preserved. But every test header already has a fixed spelling, and none checks a mixed-case name against the stored one.

items.label: Is header-name case preserved after delete and re-add?
items.ask: Does `_normalize_header_values` preserve the exact header-name case of a folded header when it deletes and re-adds it on the `HTTPMessage`? What test would prove it?

items.label: Could only the changed headers be rewritten?
items.ask: Could `_normalize_header_values` rewrite only the headers whose values changed instead of deleting and re-adding all of them? What would break about ordering?

items.label: What does Requests actually read?
items.ask: Which attribute does Requests read cookies from on a urllib3 response, and does it go through `_original_response.msg`?

text.standard: The pattern is (?:(?<![ \t])[ \t]+)?\r\n[ \t]+. It reads as an optional run of leading whitespace (OWS), then the CRLF, then required trailing whitespace (RWS). Each match is replaced with one space . The (?<![ \t]) lookbehind means the optional OWS group can only begin at the first character of a space/tab run. A comment in the diff says this avoids quadratic backtracking .

Why the lookbehind is needed. re.sub tries a match at every position. Take a value with n spaces and no CRLF after them, such as "a" + " " * n + "b", which could only reach the regex if some other part of the value held a . Without the lookbehind, [ ]+ would start at each of the n positions. Each attempt would greedily consume to the end of the run, fail to find , and give back one character at a time. That is O(n²) in total. With the lookbehind, only the first position of the run runs the greedy match, which costs O(n) including its backtracking. Every later position inside the run fails the lookbehind straight away, and the engine moves on. The cost is linear in the run length. The fast path, which skips the regex when the value has no , already protects ordinary values. The lookbehind covers hostile values that do contain a fold somewhere . The linear-time claim follows from this reasoning. The tests do not time it, so no test would catch a regression.

Why this gives one space per fold. The match consumes the OWS before the CRLF, the CRLF, and all the RWS after it. The single replacement space stands in for all of that. This is what RFC 9112 asks for, since each obs-fold becomes one space. The lookbehind does not lose any whitespace. Matching goes left to right, so the leading run is always matched from its first character. "before \t\r\n\t after" becomes "before after" .

Adjacent folds show the consequence. In "one three", the first match takes including its RWS. The next match starts at the following , with no OWS left to absorb. It takes . The result is "one three", with two spaces, one per fold . A regex that treated the whole region as a single whitespace run would give one space. That would be the wrong reading of "replace each obs-fold". The repeated-fold socket case asserts the same behaviour on the wire: one two three becomes one two three .

What the pattern does not touch. A bare \r\n not followed by a space or tab is not a fold, because the RWS part requires at least one character. The pattern leaves it alone, and _normalize_header_value returns it unchanged. Ordinary whitespace inside a value, such as "one\t two", is also preserved, since the pattern only fires around a CRLF .

items.label: Can a value like `"a\r\nb"` (a CRLF not followed by a space or tab) still reach `HTTPHeaderDict`?
items.ask: Can a header value containing a CRLF that is not followed by a space or tab survive `_normalize_header_value`, and could that still produce raw CRLF in `HTTPHeaderDict`?

items.label: Is there a test that would fail if the lookbehind were removed?
items.ask: Which test, if any, would fail if the `(?<![ \t])` lookbehind were deleted from `_OBSOLETE_FOLD_RE`, and how could a timing test be written?

items.label: How does `_normalize_header_values` treat a value that was already normalized?
items.ask: In `_normalize_header_values`, what happens when no value changes, and is the delete-and-re-add path skipped entirely?

cards.title: How the tests cover edge cases

text.standard: The tests cover the whitespace around obs-fold fairly thoroughly. They cover header-name cases not at all, and the changelog and description say that is deliberate.

Whitespace combinations. The socket-level test sends four headers, one for each pairing of trailing whitespace before the CRLF (SP or HTAB) with leading whitespace after it (SP or HTAB). Each must come back as before after. A fifth header, Fold-Mixed-Repeated, mixes runs of both kinds across two folds and must come back as one two three. The Set-Cookie fold has four leading spaces on its continuation line, so a run longer than one character is covered too. The test is written at the socket level because it sends raw bytes. This means the real http.client parser produces the folded values, rather than the test hand-building an HTTPMessage.
Unit cases for _normalize_header_value. The four parametrized cases pin down what the regex consumes.

items.html: ordinary\tvalue has no CRLF, so it stays unchanged. This exercises the fast path.
before \t\r\n\t after shows that whitespace on both sides of the CRLF collapses to a single space.
one\r\n two\t\r\n\tthree is two folds in one value, giving one space each.

one\r\n \r\n\tthree becomes one three, with two spaces. The first fold's trailing whitespace is consumed with its own CRLF, and the second fold starts at the next CRLF. So adjacent folds each produce one space, and nothing merges or disappears. This is the case that tests "one space per fold, not zero".

text.standard: The socket test also checks that Ordinary: one\t two keeps its internal tab and space. That shows the regex only touches whitespace that is attached to a CRLF.

Message-level cases. test_normalize_header_values_preserves_message covers duplicate Set-Cookie entries interleaved with other headers. It checks that the returned items and message.items() match the expected order, and that the payload, defects and policy keep their identity. This guards the delete-and-re-add rewrite. The socket test also checks HTTPHeaderDict and _original_response.msg agree.
What is not covered.

items.html: Header-name cases: whitespace before the colon, and names with odd characters. This is intentionally out of scope.
Header names with mixed case through delete and re-add. The unit test uses Set-Cookie and X-First in their usual casing, so case preservation is not demonstrated.
A bare \n fold, or a fold with no whitespace after the CRLF. The regex needs \r\n followed by at least one SP or HTAB, and no test shows other line endings being left alone.
A very long whitespace run. The (?<![ \t]) lookbehind exists to avoid quadratic backtracking, but no test would catch a regression to it.

items.label: Does a mixed-case header name survive the delete-and-re-add loop?
items.ask: In `_normalize_header_values`, does `del message[name]` followed by `message[name] = value` preserve the original header-name case, and is there a test for it?

items.label: Could a timing test cover the quadratic-backtracking case?
items.ask: How would I write a test that fails if `_OBSOLETE_FOLD_RE` loses its `(?<![ \t])` lookbehind on a long whitespace run?

items.label: What happens to a lone `\r\n` with no following whitespace?
items.ask: What does `_normalize_header_value` do with a value containing `\r\n` that is not followed by a space or tab?

cards.title: Effects on Requests and other consumers

text.standard: Two objects come out of getresponse with header data: the HTTPHeaderDict on the urllib3 response, and the stdlib HTTPMessage (httplib_response.msg). Before the change both held the raw \r\n, because HTTPHeaderDict was built straight from msg.items(). Fixing only the HTTPHeaderDict would leave the second copy dirty. The description says cookie consumers such as Requests read the original message, so they would still see the CRLF and could re-emit it when serialising the next request.

The change handles this by having _normalize_header_values write the normalized values back into the same HTTPMessage object. It deletes every header and re-adds them in order, and it does this only when some value changed. The message keeps its identity, so any reference a consumer already holds sees the unfolded values. The socket-level test checks this from the consumer side. It asserts that r._original_response.msg.get_all("set-cookie") returns the unfolded cookies and that msg["fold-mixed-repeated"] is "one two three". It also asserts that headers is msg, so the response's headers attribute and its msg are the same object.

The alternative was to leave the stdlib object alone and have consumers read HTTPHeaderDict only. That does not help Requests-style code that goes through _original_response. The reason for the in-place write is therefore the author's stated one: keeping the two views identical. The cost is that urllib3 now mutates an object that belongs to the standard library. If the rewrite were skipped, the folded Set-Cookie from #1362 would reach a cookie jar with its CRLF intact.

The repository does not contain Requests. How Requests reads cookies, and how it serialises the next request, comes from the PR description, which lists end-to-end checks of both.  I did not verify those checks myself. The in-repo evidence is the two-view equality asserted in the socket test, not a Requests run.

items.ask: Is there a way to unfold obs-fold for `_original_response.msg` consumers without deleting and re-adding every header on the stdlib HTTPMessage?

items.label: What breaks if a consumer holds a reference to `msg` before `getresponse` returns?
items.ask: Can anything read httplib_response.msg between parsing and `_normalize_header_values` running, and would it see the raw CRLF?

items.label: Does the delete-and-re-add rewrite preserve header-name case?
items.ask: Does `_normalize_header_values` preserve the original header-name case, and which test would show it?

pages.title: Bare-LF folds bypass unfolding
pages.summary: Only CRLF folds are detected, so a bare-LF fold would probably leave a raw newline in both HTTPHeaderDict and the HTTPMessage.

text.standard: The fast path and the regex only recognise CRLF folds. _normalize_header_value returns early unless "\r\n" is in the value. _OBSOLETE_FOLD_RE also requires \r\n.

http.client parses headers with the email parser under the compat32 policy. As I recall, that policy keeps whatever line ending a continuation line had. It only strips a trailing from the whole value. I did not run it, so a server that folds with a bare (Set-Cookie: a=1 b=2) would probably leave "a=1 b=2" in the value. The fast path would skip it.
The tests only send CRLF folds. The final assertion checks that no \r or \n remains, but only for those inputs. The unit parametrization has no bare-LF case.
The description and changelog say folded lines no longer leave raw line breaks in values.

The invariant "no raw line break in header values" holds only for CRLF folds. A bare-LF fold would still put a raw \n into both HTTPHeaderDict and the original HTTPMessage, which is the same cookie re-emission hazard the PR targets. A hostile server controls the bytes, so this is reachable. Confidence is medium because I have not run the parser.
To close it, either:

items.html: widen the pattern to \r?\n, or
state that only CRLF folds are handled.

text.standard: Add a socket-level case that sends a bare-LF fold either way.

pages.title: Adjacent-fold wording and untested linear-time claim
pages.summary: The description says adjacent folds give one space but the test expects two; the no-quadratic-backtracking claim has no long-input test.

text.standard: The description says adjacent folds collapse to one space, not zero. The unit test expects the opposite: "one\r\n \r\n\tthree" gives "one three", with two spaces. The regex consumes one fold at a time, so each fold becomes its own space.
The comment on the regex claims it avoids quadratic backtracking for long values.  No test sends a long whitespace run or a long folded value. The only inputs are short strings.

The code is consistent with the RFC, which allows one or more SP per fold. The description is wrong about adjacent folds, and the test pins the two-space result. That is a documentation mismatch, not a bug.

The linear-time claim looks right from reading the lookbehind, but it is untested. This is a test gap, not a bug. To close it, correct the description wording. Optionally add a test with a long whitespace run, such as 100k spaces followed by \r\n x, or one with no fold, and assert it finishes quickly.

A fold is a CRLF (\r\n) that is directly followed by at least one space or tab. The CRLF alone doesn't make it a fold. The whitespace after it is what tells the parser that the next line continues the previous header instead of starting a new one. RFC 9112 calls this obs-fold, which is optional whitespace, then CRLF, then required whitespace (OWS CRLF RWS).

That is exactly what _OBSOLETE_FOLD_RE matches. The required part is \r\n[ \t]+, and the leading (?:(?<![ \t])[ \t]+)? is the optional whitespace before the CRLF. Each match is replaced with a single space.
The "followed by whitespace" part has two consequences:

items.html: A CRLF with no whitespace after it is not a fold. The pattern requires at least one space or tab, so _normalize_header_value leaves such a value alone.

The whitespace is consumed along with the CRLF. The continuation line's leading whitespace, such as the four spaces in the socket test's Set-Cookie, disappears into the one replacement space. The result is ___utmvbtouVBFmB=gZg XbNOjalT: ....

text.standard: The detector only recognises \r\n. The fast path returns early unless "\r\n" is in the value. The critic finding about bare-LF folds is about this gap, and I haven't run the parser to confirm it.
